conservation.notes: Least Concern, on the basis of an extensive range, an increasing population trend and a large population size. North American Breeding Bird Survey and Christmas Bird Count data indicate a significant increase of 82.9% over 40 years. The species is labelled invasive by some organizations.

human_tolerance.notes: Native to Mexico and the southwestern United States, the species was released in the eastern United States in the 1940s as 'Hollywood finches' and has become naturalized, and in largely unforested land 'they have displaced the native purple finch and even the non-native house sparrow'. It is a frequent feeder visitor year-round and nests in cavities including building openings and hanging plants.

phases.name: nesting
phases.note: 'The female lays clutches of eggs from February through August, two or more broods per year with 2 to 6 eggs per brood, most commonly 4 or 5', incubating for 12 to 14 days.

phases.name: young
phases.note: The male is the primary feeder of the fledglings, which can be told from females by pin feathers remaining on their heads; nests may be re-used for subsequent broods or in following years.

vocalizations.description: A series of high-pitched musical jumbles ending with a distinct high note, 'wheer'.
A soft 'cheet' or 'wheat' given in flight, with perched birds giving a more drawn-out version.

taxonomy.note: GBIF's match returns Haemorhous mexicanus (Statius Müller, 1776) as ACCEPTED; the article's lead places the species 'in the genus Haemorhous' with the other two American rosefinches. Family Fringillidae is the article's.

external.note: gbif_usage_key is the ACCEPTED key from the GBIF species match for Haemorhous mexicanus; inat_taxon_id is the iNaturalist taxon returned by the API match. Optional keys (ITIS TSN, Wikidata Q-number, eBird code) were not looked up, so they are omitted rather than guessed.

conservation.note: 'assessed as "Least Concern" on the IUCN Red List due to its extensive range, increasing population trend, and large population size'. The 82.9% forty-year increase is the article's own figure from Breeding Bird Survey and Christmas Bird Count data. The article's statement that 'The species is labeled as invasive by some organizations' is recorded rather than resolved, because the article does not name which organizations.

range.note: 'native to Mexico and southwestern United States, but has since been introduced to the eastern part of North America and Hawai'i', and 'found year-round in almost all parts of the United States and most of Mexico, with breeding grounds well into Canada as far north as northern Alberta'. US and MX are native; CA is given as introduced on the strength of the stated release history and the Canadian breeding range. The Hawaii and Spain naturalizations are deliberately not listed, because the record's region list is meant to stay small and the Hawaii codes were not checked against the schema's RegionCode pattern here. koppen is omitted: the article names urban, suburban and semi-open western habitat but gives no climate classification.

traits.mass_kg.note: 'with an average weight of 21 g (3/4 oz)'. The article's own average, recorded unsmoothed.

traits.mass_range_kg.note: 'Body mass can vary from 16 to 27 g (9/16 to 15/16 oz)'.

traits.length_m.note: Midpoint of '12.5 to 15 cm (5 to 6 in) long'.

traits.wingspan_m.note: Midpoint of 'a wingspan of 20 to 25 cm (8 to 10 in)'.

traits.lifespan_y.note: Honest gap, borrowed with a reason: the article gives no lifespan figure, but its account of reproduction is unusually complete - 'two or more broods per year with 2 to 6 eggs per brood, most commonly 4 or 5' - and a small, prolific, short-lived cavity-nesting granivore of this kind typically does not survive long. 2.2 y is set from the sourced house sparrow record already in this repository (Passer domesticus, ~2.2 y from survival statistics), which is a similar-sized, similarly prolific, similarly urban granivore. The value is an inference from a close analogue, not a figure for this species, and a reviewer should replace it if a ringing study for Haemorhous mexicanus becomes available.

traits.diet.note: 'They primarily eat grains, seeds and berries, being voracious consumers of weed seeds such as nettle and dandelion; included are incidental small insects such as aphids.' seed 0.6 and fruit 0.3 follow the named staples, with fruit carrying the berries and the grain-and-weed-seed share between them; invertebrate 0.1 reflects the article's own word 'incidental' for the insects.

traits.social.note: 'They are frequent visitors to bird feeders throughout the year' and 'will congregate at hanging nyjer sock feeders', which is the flocking the record needs; the male feeds the female through courtship, incubation and rearing, so a pair bond exists within that group structure.

traits.activity_pattern.note: Judgement: diurnal. Foraging at feeders and in vegetation, nest building and singing are all described by day, and no nocturnal activity is described.

traits.defense.note: The article describes no aggressive defence of the nest and instead records cavity nesting in places 'including openings in buildings, hanging plants, and other cup-shaped outdoor decorations', where the bird relies on concealment; Flee is recorded on that basis.

traits.nest_type.note: 'Nests are made in cavities, including openings in buildings, hanging plants, and other cup-shaped outdoor decorations. Sometimes nests abandoned by other birds are used.' Cavity is the matching enum value, even though the nest itself is a cup, because the site is what the enum describes.

traits.perching.note: 'Calls from flight include a soft cheet or wheat, with perched birds giving a more drawn-out version', and the bird forages 'in vegetation' as well as on the ground; perching on vegetation to sing and feed is the ordinary posture.

traits.note: Grouped entries. body_plan Vertebrate, limb_count 2, thermoregulation Endotherm, skin Feathers, respiration Lungs and metamorphosis None are the standard bird values the article's description of a finch implies. flight Powered follows the bird's movement between feeding, nesting and roosting sites. size_class Tiny is derived from mass_kg (under 0.05 kg). locomotion_modes Walk, Hop and Fly: the bird forages on the ground and in vegetation, hops between perches, and flies between sites.

traits.wariness.note: Judgement set low: 'House finches forage on the ground or in vegetation normally', 'are frequent visitors to bird feeders throughout the year', and nest 'in cavities, including openings in buildings, hanging plants, and other cup-shaped outdoor decorations' in urban and suburban habitat. flight_distance_m 25 m reflects a feeder-habituated bird that leaves rather than hides.

habitat.use.note: Authored from the feeding, habitat and breeding sections: 'forage on the ground or in vegetation normally' in 'urban and suburban areas ... as well as various semi-open areas in the west', nesting in cavities in buildings, hanging plants and other garden structures. Vegetation and buildings therefore slightly exceed bare ground use.

habitat.shelter_tag.note: 'Nests are made in cavities, including openings in buildings, hanging plants, and other cup-shaped outdoor decorations', sometimes in nests abandoned by other birds. cavity is the matching ResourceTag and the dependence is total.

habitat.resources.note: The weights follow traits.diet, with the incidental insect share kept small to match the article's wording. cavity 1.0 reflects total nesting dependence on a cavity. perch 0.7 reflects perching in vegetation to sing and feed.

habitat.human_tolerance.note: Exploiter and uses_gardens are quoted almost directly: 'Their breeding habitat is urban and suburban areas across North America', 'They are frequent visitors to bird feeders throughout the year', and the species nests in building openings and hanging plants. The introduction history is recorded in the notes because it explains both the tolerance and the species' displacement of native finches in eastern North America. light_max 0.7 and flight_distance_m 25 m are authored judgements for a bird that feeds in the open beside people.

seasonal.strategy.note: 'House finches are mainly permanent residents throughout their range; some birds migrate to the south, with adult females moving longer distances than males.' PartialMigration is the enum value for a resident species with partial southward movement; the split between the many birds that stay and the females that move is not quantified, so winter_fraction 0.6 is an authored estimate meaning roughly that most of a northern population overwinters in place. A reviewer should replace this with a band-recovery figure if one becomes available.

seasonal.phases.note: 'The female lays clutches of eggs from February through August, two or more broods per year with 2 to 6 eggs per brood, most commonly 4 or 5', and 'The female incubates the eggs for 12 to 14 days'. The young window runs from the first possible hatching under that incubation to the end of the stated laying period plus one brood cycle, because the male is recorded as 'the primary feeder of the fledglings'. Month boundaries here are quoted from the article rather than authored, which is unusual and worth noting as the article's own calendar.

seasonal.life_stages.note: Egg duration is the stated '12 to 14 days' of incubation. The article says the young 'are silent for the first seven or eight days, and subsequently start peeping during feedings' but gives no nestling or fledgling duration, so the Juvenile duration of 21 days is an authored judgement for a small finch, flagged as such rather than quoted. scale is authored.

vocalizations.wheer_song.note: 'The house finch's songs typically consist of a series of high-pitched musical jumbles ending with a distinct high note, wheer.' Quoted directly. Months are restricted to the February-August laying period the article gives, on the reasoning that a resident pair sings through its breeding cycle; time windows and the cooldown are authored, as no open source gives them. No open source gives frequency bands.

vocalizations.cheet.note: 'Calls from flight include a soft cheet or wheat, with perched birds giving a more drawn-out version.' Quoted directly, and mapped to the schema's Contact context, the closest enum value to the species' ordinary call. Time windows and the cooldown are authored.

look.note: Colours from the description section: 'Adults have a long, square-tipped brown tail and are a brown or dull-brown color across the back with some shading into deep gray on the wing feathers. Breast and belly feathers may be streaked; the flanks usually are. In most cases, adult males' heads, necks and shoulders are reddish', ranging 'from pale straw-yellow through bright orange (both rare) to deep, intense red'. The palette maps brown to body, the pale streaked underparts to belly, the darker wing and tail markings to markings, and accent holds the male's red head colour, which the red_crown extra part places on the head. The record is modelled on an adult male, the more distinctive sex, which the article says females 'are typically attracted to ... males with the deepest pigment of red'. Proportions are otherwise authored.

behavior.note: Authored parameters for the shared perching-songbird program: food_tag seed rather than the program's invertebrate default, because this species is a grain, seed and berry eater that visits feeders; a short flee distance for a bird habituated to people; a February-August nest window matching the article's unusually long laying season; and call ids matching the two vocalizations above. The program is a good fit for a small perching cavity-nesting finch.
